## Coding to do statistics!

This activity is based in a programming language called `R`. It was developed by two statistics instructors in New Zealand, so it is designed specifically for data analysis. Now it is used around the world by people doing statistics and data science in all kinds of fields.

The focus of this activity isn't learning every detail of the code. Instead, you'll be using code to investigate a dataset, and the questions will focus your attention on certain key parts of the code and analysis as you go.

Let's get started!

## Palmer Penguins

We're going to look at a built-in dataset in R called `penguins`. It includes data about three species of penguins that live in the Palmer Archipelago, a set of Antarctic islands south of South America.

![Three species of Palmer Archipelago penguins. Artwork by \@allison_horst.](images/penguins.png){fig-alt="Three penguins, one labeled Chinstrap, one labeled Gentoo, and one labeled Adelie." width="380"}

Let's start by making a table of how many penguins of each species are in this dataset.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Press the “Run code” button below to make a table.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: species
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

count(penguins, species)

```

::: callout-note
Code is text written in a certain way to tell the computer what to do when we "run" the code.
:::

This code chunk used a **function** named `count` to count up the number of penguins of each species in the dataset. To do this, the computer needed to know what data to look at -- that's the `penguins` dataset -- and what **variable** within the dataset to look at. In this case, the variable we used was `species`. We wanted to give these two pieces of information to the function `count`, which is why they were in the parentheses `()` after the function name.

```{code-blanks-response}
What does the `n` column of the output table tell us?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
What species of penguin was most common in the dataset?
```

## What else can we count?

There are several other categorical variables in the penguins dataset, including `island` and `sex`.

Fill in the blank in the code below and then press "Run code" to make a table of the number of penguins in the dataset from each island.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: island
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

count(penguins, island)

```

We might want to split our observations by multiple categorical variables. Press "Run code" to make a table of the penguins in the dataset split by `island` and `sex`.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: sex
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

count(penguins, island, sex)

```

```{code-blanks-response}
In 1-2 sentences, describe the key takeaways from the results in the table above.
```

```{code-blanks-response}
If we wrote `count(penguins, sex, island)` instead, what would be different about the table? Why might we choose one order over the other?
```

Fill in and run the code below to make a table showing the number of penguins of each species on each island.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|  target: island
#|  prefill: false
#|  occurrence: 1
#|  match: text
#| blank:
#|  target: species
#|  prefill: false
#|  occurrence: 1
#|  match: text

count(penguins, island, species)
```


## Graphing our results

Tables are useful, but sometimes a visual like a graph is a more succinct way of communicating that information.

The most appropriate graphical representation of categorical data like this is a **bar graph**. Let's start with a bar graph that considers a single variable, `species`.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: species
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = species) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Number of Penguins"
  )

```

The code for making a graph has several **layers**. The first, `ggplot`, sets up the canvas for plotting, and we tell it the dataset we'll be using. The second, `aes`, is named after "aesthetics," so this is mapping visual features of the graph to variables in our dataset. The third is the geometry, in this case `geom_bar`. Each type of graph corresponds to a geometry. Finally, we end with `labs`, named after "labels," where we add the title and axis labels.

```{code-blanks-response}
Why do we use `x = species` as the argument to `aes` for this graph?
```

Suppose I want a horizontal bar graph instead of a vertical one. Fill in and run the code below to make the same graph as above, but with horizontal bars.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: y = species
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(y = species) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Number of Penguins",
    y = "Penguin Species"
  )

```

Bar graphs can give us information about multiple categories. There are a couple of different ways to do this. The first is called a **multiple bar graph.**

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: fill = sex
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: position = "dodge"
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = species, fill = sex) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Number of Penguins",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
How did this multiple bar chart show both `species` and `island`?
```

Make a multiple bar chart showing the number of penguins by species and island.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: fill = island
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: position = "dodge"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = species, fill = island) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Number of Penguins",
    fill = "Island"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
Why do some species only have one bar?
```

Another way to show two variables in a bar chart is with a **stacked bar chart**. Run the example below.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: "stack"
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = species, fill = sex) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack") +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Number of Penguins",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
How did this stacked bar chart show both `species` and `island`?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
What changed in the code between the multiple bar chart and the stacked bar chart?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
When do you think a multiple bar chart would be better? When would a stacked bar chart be better?
```

Finally, sometimes we're more interested in percentages than in counts, so we can use a filled bar chart.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: "fill"
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = species, fill = sex) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Proportion of Each Sex",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
What value of `position` was used for this filled bar chart?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
What information does this chart give us that is **clearer** than in the other graphs? What information does this graph **not** give us?
```

Change the code below to make a graph of your choosing with two variables chosen from `species`, `island`, and `sex`. The graph should be different from any of the ones above and correctly labeled. Feel free to try several different formats to see what you think best communicates key results!

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|  target: "blank1"
#|  prefill: false
#|  occurrence: 1
#|  match: text

#| blank:
#|  target: "blank2"
#|  prefill: false

#|  prefill: false

#| blank:

#| blank:

ggplot(penguins) +
```


Congratulations! You can now make clear frequency tables and bar graphs in `R` to summarize categorical data!
